title: An ignition-delay grid is read as lines on a 1000/T plot, and a stirred-reactor curve as a response that jumps once the reactor ignites
summary: The ignition-delay figure shows time to ignition against inverse temperature in three pressure panels; the reactor figure shows the steady water mole fraction of a stirred reactor against temperature. Both are model outputs, so the reading is about shape, slope and gaps, not about agreement with data.

media.alt: Three side-by-side log-scale panels of ignition delay in microseconds against 1000 over T from 0.36 to 1.0, for pressures 0.1 atm, 3.16 atm and 100 atm, with six coloured curves for equivalence ratio 0.3, 1 and 6 at 50 and 90 percent dilution. At 100 atm all curves rise smoothly and almost in parallel toward low temperature; at 0.1 atm some curves rise and then fall, with humps near 1000/T equal to 0.75.

source.caption: Ignition-delay grid, Ar dilution
source.note: Group explainer. Both are simulations of the bundled hydrogen mechanism file named in the title (Cantera h2o2_he.yaml); no experimental data are on either panel set.
group: 06_07_jsr_scurve_AR: JSR S-curve, Ar dilution: steady H2O mole fraction against temperature at three pressures

read_the_figure.question: How does the model's ignition delay depend on temperature, pressure, mixture and dilution, and at what temperature does a stirred reactor jump to its burning state?
read_the_figure.axes: Ignition grid: x is 1000/T in 1/K from about 0.36 (T about 2800 K) to 1.0 (1000 K), hot on the left; y is the ignition delay tau_ig in microseconds on a log scale; one panel per pressure (0.1, 3.16228 and 100 atm); curves are equivalence ratios 0.3, 1 and 6 at 50 and 90 percent dilution. Reactor figure: x is temperature 700 to 1400 K; y is the steady-state mole fraction of H2O on a log scale from 1e-12 to 1; panels are 0.1, 1 and 10 atm; curves are phi = 0.3, 1 and 6; residence time 100 ms, 50 percent Ar.
look_at: 100 atm panel: curves rise smoothly and almost in parallel toward low temperature: a nearly straight band on this plot is the signature of one activation energy.
0.1 atm panel: curves bend, flatten and some turn back down near 1000/T of 0.75: a non-monotonic dependence, expected for hydrogen at low pressure where chain branching and termination compete.
Compare the three panels: the delay spans many decades between the hot and the cold ends, and the curves cross at the lower pressures.

Reactor figure: the water fraction rises by more than ten decades between 700 and 900 K and then flattens: the reactor has ignited and sits on its burning branch. At 0.1 atm the rise is steeper and shows an overshoot near 790 K.
read_the_figure.proves: That the model produces smooth, physically shaped responses over a large range of conditions. Without measured points on the same axes it cannot prove the model is right.
if_wrong: Curves with no markers hide where the computed points are: a smooth line may be a fit or an interpolation.
Curves that stop (as the phi = 6, 90 percent curve at 0.1 atm does) mean no ignition was found in the time bound or the run failed at those temperatures.
A reactor curve that is single-valued cannot show the hysteresis that gives an S-curve its name.
must_check: Experimental points are overlaid when the figure is used for validation: none are.
The ignition criterion (for example peak temperature gradient) is stated: it is not.
The reactor start state is stated: here 'cold-started per T', a single branch.
Computed points are marked, not only a line through them.

The right quantity is on the right axis: the page calls the reactor figure an S-curve of residence time against temperature, but the axes are the steady H2O fraction against temperature at a fixed residence time.
as_drawn: Ignition delay at 100 atm spans from about 0.02 microseconds at the hot end to about 1e4 microseconds at 1000 K (read by eye); delays below 1 microsecond at the hot end are very short and worth checking against the ignition definition.
The phi = 6, 90 percent dilution curve at 0.1 atm starts at about 1000/T = 0.52 (about 1900 K): it is absent on the hot side.
Reactor figure: at 0.1 atm the phi = 6 curve peaks near 0.5 at about 790 K, then dips and settles near 0.07; at 1 and 10 atm the curves are smooth and monotone.

terms.meaning: The time from the start of a constant-volume or constant-pressure run until ignition occurs, defined by a criterion such as the steepest temperature rise.
A plot of the logarithm of a rate or time against 1/T. A straight line has a slope proportional to an activation energy.
The fraction of the mixture that is inert bath gas (here argon). It lowers the heat release and the reactivity.
A reactor whose contents are assumed perfectly mixed, fed continuously. Its steady state balances reaction against throughflow.
The average time a fluid parcel spends in the reactor: volume over volumetric flow.
The S-shaped plot of steady state against a control parameter, with an unstable middle branch and a jump from an extinguished to an ignited branch.
Starting the reactor from unreacted gas at each temperature. It follows the lower branch until it jumps to the burning one.

remember: On a 1000/T axis a straight line is an activation energy; its slope in decades per unit is E_a / (2.303 R) times 1000.
Hot is on the left of a 1000/T axis.
Hydrogen ignition delay can be non-monotonic at low pressure; a bend is not necessarily an error.
A reactor that jumps to its burning branch gives a very steep rise on a log axis.
A simulation-only figure shows model behaviour, not model correctness.

understand.title: Reading the grid
understand.text: Each panel is a family of nearly parallel lines at high pressure and a more tangled family at low pressure. Lines that move up or down with phi and dilution show the sensitivity of the delay to the mixture; the spacing between panels shows pressure sensitivity.

understand.title: What the humps mean
understand.text: At 0.1 atm the delay does not simply fall as the temperature rises: chain-branching and chain-terminating steps compete and their balance shifts with temperature and pressure. A hump is a signature of that competition, which is why validation near such regions is demanding.

understand.title: The reactor curve
understand.text: At low temperature the reactor holds almost nothing but fresh gas, so the water fraction is tiny and rises exponentially with temperature. Once heat release exceeds heat loss the reactor jumps to a burning state with a nearly constant water fraction set by the mixture. The jump is the steep rise.

steps.title: Arrhenius form of the delay
steps.note: Taking logs turns the exponential into a straight line in 1/T. The slope is E_a over R.

steps.title: Converting the slope to an activation energy
steps.note: Reading the slope of a log10 axis in decades per unit of 1000/T and multiplying by R ln 10 times 1000 gives an apparent activation energy; a curved line has a slope that changes with T.

steps.title: Perfectly stirred reactor balance
steps.note: Species production by reaction against replacement by the feed. At steady state the left side is zero.

steps.title: Steady state by a balance of heat
steps.note: The generation term is a steep sigmoid in T, the loss term is a straight line. Their intersections are the steady states; with three intersections the curve is S-shaped.

steps.title: Why the cold start jumps
steps.note: Increasing T the low branch disappears at a tangency and the state jumps to the burning branch: the steep rise in the reactor figure. Running back down from the burning branch would show a different extinction point.

steps.title: Why the jump is steep on a log axis
steps.note: Below ignition the product forms at a rate with an effective activation energy, so on a log axis it climbs like an Arrhenius line (about ten decades here); above it the burning branch is flat.

steps.title: Counting temperature
steps.note: The conversion between the x axis and temperature that the figure does not show with ticks.

worked.title: Apparent activation energy from a slope
worked.problem: A straight line on a 1000/T plot falls by 3 decades of tau (base 10) over a change of 0.5 in 1000/T. What is the apparent activation energy? (Illustrative numbers, not from the figure.)

solution.text: Slope in decades per unit of 1000/T.
Convert: E_a / R = slope times ln 10 times 1000.

worked.answer: About 115 kJ/mol. Real delay curves bend, so the slope, and the apparent energy, change along the curve.

analyze.q: Compare the 100 atm and 0.1 atm panels. What does the loss of near-parallel lines at low pressure tell you about the number of controlling reaction steps?
analyze.hint: A single activation energy gives parallel lines; competing steps do not.

analyze.q: Why can the reactor figure not display hysteresis? What would you add to show it?
analyze.hint: Cold start from fresh gas gives one branch; start from a burning state and ramp down for the other.

analyze.q: The phi = 6, 90 percent dilution curve is missing on the hot side at 0.1 atm. List two causes and one check for each.
analyze.hint: No ignition within the bound; failed solve; undefined criterion.

evaluate.q: The page calls the reactor figure an S-curve of residence time. Judge whether the plotted quantities support that name.
evaluate.hint: A single-branch response at one residence time is not the multivalued plot of an S-curve.

evaluate.q: Suppose the ignition delays below 1 microsecond at the hot end are suspect. What definition or unit check would you do?
evaluate.hint: Ignition criterion, time-step output, units of the axis label.

create: Redraw the delay grid with markers at the computed temperatures and one experimental dataset overlaid.
Design the figure that would show the S-curve: the control parameter, the two sweep directions, and the branches.

checks.q: Why is the ignition-delay axis logarithmic and the x axis 1000/T?
checks.hint: A rate with an activation energy.
checks.answer: Because tau is roughly A exp(E_a / R T): taking logs makes it linear in 1/T, so slopes give activation energies and delays that span many decades fit on one axis.

checks.q: A line falls by 2 decades over 0.4 in 1000/T. What is its slope in decades per unit?
Why is a hump in an ignition-delay curve plausible for hydrogen at low pressure?
checks.answer: Chain-branching and chain-terminating reactions have different temperature and pressure dependences, and at low pressure their balance changes with temperature, so the net rate, and hence the delay, can change direction.

checks.q: Does a smooth model curve show that the model is valid?
checks.answer: No. Smoothness shows the model is well-behaved. Validity needs experimental points on the same axes.

checks.q: How would you make the reactor figure show the S shape?
checks.answer: Sweep the control parameter upward from an unreacted state and downward from a burning state, plot both, and show the unstable middle branch with a continuation method.
